The Next War with Iran Could Escalate Almost Immediately, and Far Beyond the Previous Conflict 

One thing has become increasingly clear from Iran’s behavior in recent weeks: if the confrontation returns to full-scale war, escalation is likely to be rapid, dramatic, and potentially far more dangerous than anything we witnessed during the previous conflict.

The red lines that constrained both sides during the last war could collapse almost immediately. We should not assume that another confrontation would begin with gradual escalation, carefully calibrated retaliation, or attempts to signal intentions while avoiding a broader conflict.

Quite the opposite. Once either side decides to return to high-intensity warfare, the conflict could escalate dramatically from the very beginning.

Even if the next war lasts fewer than 39 days, its intensity could be significantly greater from day one, as both sides seek to apply the lessons they believe they learned from the previous confrontation.

From Tehran’s perspective, this could mean expanding the geographical boundaries of the conflict, targeting critical infrastructure, including undersea internet cables, and potentially even considering limited ground operations toward Kuwait.

These are not inevitable outcomes, but they are scenarios that should no longer be dismissed.

The fundamental danger is that the next war may not follow the familiar pattern of action, retaliation, and gradual escalation. Instead, both sides could move almost immediately toward their most aggressive military options, believing that the lessons of the previous war demand precisely that approach.

The next war with Iran may be shorter than the last one. But it could also be far more intense, destructive, and difficult to contain from the very first day.

text:
At the end of September, I wrote that the market was incorrectly assuming that the Oman Lane flows would continue. Financial writers were so eager to proclaim that 1) Iran lost control and 2) oil flows are going back to normal. That turned out to be a very bad call.

The reality right now is that the Oman Lane transit flows continue. As of the latest figures I’ve seen, implied Strait of Hormuz flow is somewhere between 8 and 9 million b/d, down from 13-14 million b/d. The forward-looking implied flow (over the next 10 days) is expected to fall to 6-7 million b/d.

For the moment, oil traders continue to see the latest attacks as transitory. We are not seeing any material panic in the physical market just yet. The surge in crude volumes out of the Strait of Hormuz in mid-September is enough to calm things down a bit just as global refineries enter maintenance this time of the year, but I suspect elevated tanker rates are masking some of the inherent panic to come.

OPEC has cut its 2026 oil demand growth forecast to just 180,000 barrels per day (kb/d), while raising its 2027 projection to 2.55 million barrels per day (mb/d), pointing to a sharp recovery in consumption next year. The organisation also reported a 920 kb/d increase in September OPEC production to 25.1 mb/d, approaching pre-war levels, as higher output from Saudi Arabia and Iraq more than offset declines elsewhere.

However, a substantial gap remains between OPEC's relatively optimistic outlook and the considerably more bearish assessments from the EIA and IEA. In its latest Short-Term Energy Outlook, the EIA projected a 2 mb/d contraction in demand this year, compared with the 2.5 mb/d decline forecast by the IEA in September.

The divergence highlights the exceptional uncertainty surrounding the demand impact of the Middle East disruption, particularly the extent to which elevated energy prices, supply shortages and weaker economic activity are destroying consumption. Attention now turns to the IEA's October Oil Market Report, due tomorrow, for an updated assessment of both demand destruction and the recovery in Middle East supplies.
